title: Job Offers & Negotiating
description: Read an offer, compare two, and ask for more without flinching.
wolfLine: The first number is an opening, not a verdict.

offer-letter.definition: The written job offer: title, pay, start date and benefits.

base-salary.definition: Your yearly pay before any bonuses or benefits.
base-salary.example: A $54,000 base salary plus a $2,000 signing bonus.

total-compensation.definition: Everything a job pays you in a year: base salary, bonuses and the value of benefits.

salary-range.definition: The low-to-high pay a company expects to offer for a role.

counteroffer.definition: Your polite reply to a job offer asking for more: higher pay, a bonus or more time off.
counteroffer.example: “I’m excited to join. Based on my research, could we do $56,000?”

signing-bonus.definition: A one-time payment for accepting a job offer, often with a payback rule if you leave early.
signing-bonus.example: $3,000 when you start, repaid if you leave within a year.

lessons.title: Reading an Offer Letter
lessons.summary: Before you say yes, read every line.

steps.context: An [[offer letter]] is the written job offer: title, pay, start date and benefits. Your [[base salary]] is the yearly pay before bonuses or benefits.

lines.label: 401(k) match: 100% of the first 3% you save

steps.prompt: What’s the base salary in this offer?
steps.explain: The yearly pay, before the bonus and benefits.

lines.label: 401(k) match: 100% of the first 3% you save

steps.prompt: The signing bonus is paid once. Base salary plus signing bonus: how much cash in the first year?

lines.label: 401(k) match: 100% of the first 3% you save

steps.prompt: When do you need to reply?
steps.explain: Offers often have a deadline. Ask for more time if you need it.

steps.prompt: Get the offer in writing before you quit your current job.
steps.explain: A phone promise isn’t an offer.

steps.prompt: Something in the letter differs from what they said on the phone. What do you do?
choices: Ask them to fix it in writing before you sign
Sign now and sort it out later
steps.explain: What’s written is what counts.

lines.label: 401(k) match: 100% of the first 3% you save

steps.prompt: They match 100% of the first 3% you save. If you only save 1% of $54,000, what’s the match?

lessons.title: Total Compensation
lessons.summary: The real size of an offer is more than the salary.

steps.context: [[Total compensation]] is everything a job pays you in a year: base salary, bonuses, and the value of benefits.
steps.prompt: Which counts toward total compensation?
choices: Salary, bonus and the employer’s share of benefits
steps.explain: Everything the job pays you, in cash or in benefits.

steps.prompt: Base $54,000, bonus $2,000, 401(k) match $1,620, health insurance employer share $6,000. What’s the total compensation?
Another job offers $58,000, no bonus, no match, and $3,000 toward health insurance. Total compensation?
Which offer is worth more?
steps.explain: The lower salary wins by $2,620.

steps.prompt: The job with the higher salary always pays more overall.
steps.explain: Benefits can flip it.

steps.prompt: What else matters besides total compensation?
choices: Commute, schedule, growth and how you’ll be treated
steps.explain: Money first, but not money only.

lessons.title: Know Your Number
lessons.summary: Research pay before anyone asks what you want.

steps.context: A [[salary range]] is the low-to-high pay a company expects for a role. A growing number of states require it in job postings.
steps.prompt: A posting says $48,000–$58,000. What does that tell you?
choices: Where offers for this role will likely land
steps.explain: It’s the company’s planned range.

steps.prompt: Where can you research pay for a role?
choices: Postings with ranges, salary sites, and people in the field
steps.explain: Three sources beat one.

steps.prompt: Range $48,000–$58,000. What’s the middle?
You have 3 years of experience and the role asks for 2. Where in the range should you aim?
steps.explain: You bring more than they asked for.

steps.prompt: Asking “What’s the salary range?” early in the process is reasonable.
steps.explain: It saves everyone time.

steps.prompt: They ask your current salary. What’s a safe answer?
choices: Share the range you’re looking for instead
steps.explain: Many states ban employers from asking about pay history. Either way, keep it about this job.

lessons.title: Two Offers
lessons.summary: Line them up properly, then think about your time.

steps.prompt: Northgate’s total?
How much more is Cityline worth per year?
Cityline’s commute eats about 200 more hours a year. What does that tell you?

lessons.title: How to Ask for More
lessons.summary: A polite, specific counteroffer usually helps and rarely hurts.

steps.context: A [[counteroffer]] is your polite reply asking for more: a higher salary, a bonus, more time off.
steps.prompt: When do you make a counteroffer?
choices: After you get the offer, before you accept
steps.explain: You have the most leverage between “here’s our offer” and “yes.”

steps.prompt: Put a negotiation in order.
items: Thank them and say you’re excited
Ask for a specific number, backed by research
Get the final offer in writing
steps.explain: Warm, specific, patient, written.

steps.prompt: The offer is $52,000. You ask for 6% more. What number do you ask for?
They say salary is fixed. What else can you ask about?
choices: A signing bonus, more PTO or a later start date
steps.explain: Lots of things bend when salary won’t.

steps.prompt: Politely negotiating often gets more, and rarely gets an offer taken back.
steps.explain: Employers expect it.

steps.prompt: A starting salary $3,000 higher is worth how much over 5 years, even with no other changes?

lessons.title: Bonuses & Fine Print
lessons.summary: Signing bonuses are nice. Read the strings attached.

steps.context: A [[signing bonus]] is a one-time payment for accepting an offer. It often comes with a catch: leave too soon and you pay it back.
steps.prompt: What’s a signing bonus?
choices: A one-time payment for saying yes
steps.explain: Once, not every year.

steps.prompt: A $3,000 signing bonus is taxed at about 30% when it’s paid. What lands in your account?
A signing bonus is usually taxed like regular pay.
steps.explain: It shows up on your W-2 with everything else.

steps.prompt: The letter says you repay the bonus if you leave within 12 months. You might move in 8 months. What do you do?
choices: Factor in that you might pay it back
Spend it all on day one
steps.explain: Treat it as a loan until month 12.

steps.prompt: Bonus or higher salary: which helps more over time?
choices: Higher salary: it repeats every year, and raises build on it
steps.explain: A salary bump keeps paying.

steps.prompt: A $2,000 one-time bonus vs. a salary $2,000 higher, over 4 years. How much more does the salary bump pay?

lessons.title: Job Scam Red Flags
lessons.summary: Real jobs pay you. Fake ones make you pay.

steps.context: Fake job offers are a common scam. Real employers don’t ask you to pay to start.

lines.label: Hourly pay, data entry from home
Starter equipment kit, pay by gift card

steps.prompt: Tap the biggest red flag.
steps.explain: Real employers never make you buy equipment, least of all with gift cards.

steps.prompt: They mail you a $2,400 check and ask you to deposit it and send back $1,900 for “equipment.” What happens next?
choices: The check bounces days later, and your $1,900 is gone
steps.explain: Fake checks take days to bounce. Your transfer is instant.

steps.prompt: Red flag or normal?
items: An offer with no interview at all
Asked to pay for a kit with gift cards
A background check before you start
An offer letter with salary and start date
A video interview with the team

steps.prompt: Giving your Social Security number on official new-hire paperwork is normal.
steps.explain: After you’ve accepted a real job, tax and work forms need it. Before an interview? No.

steps.prompt: How do you check a company is real?
choices: Find its official website and phone number yourself
Call the number in the suspicious text
steps.explain: Never trust contact details from the message itself.

steps.prompt: You think you’ve hit a job scam. Where do you report it?
steps.explain: Reports help warn others.

lessons.title: Nadia’s Negotiation
lessons.summary: Research, one polite email, and a better offer.

story.title: One email, $5,500
story.body:
Nadia got an offer for **$50,000**. Before replying, she looked up similar jobs in her city: most paid **$52,000–$60,000**.

She thanked them, said she was excited, and asked for **$56,000**, pointing to her research and her two years of experience.

They came back with **$54,000** plus a **$1,500** signing bonus.

steps.prompt: How much more base salary did Nadia get than the first offer?
In her first year, counting the bonus, how much more did she get?
Over 3 years, ignoring raises, how much more base salary is that?
Why did Nadia ask for $56,000 instead of $54,000?
choices: Asking a bit higher leaves room to meet in the middle
steps.explain: They met her in the middle, right where she hoped.

steps.prompt: Nadia’s research made her ask easier to justify.
steps.explain: Numbers beat feelings in a negotiation.

steps.prompt: What should Nadia do before accepting?
choices: Get the new salary and bonus in writing
Just say yes on the phone
steps.explain: Written, then signed.
